claim: The superior colliculus (SC) is a midbrain structure that receives inputs from retinal ganglion cells (RGCs).
source: The superior colliculus (SC) is a midbrain structure that receives inputs from retinal ganglion cells (RGCs).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Dräger and Hubel, 1976; Ellis et al., 2016; Huberman et al., 2008; Kremkow and Alonso, 2018)

claim: The SC contains one of the highest densities of inhibitory neurons in the brain.
source: The SC contains one of the highest densities of inhibitory neurons in the brain but whether excitatory and inhibitory SC neurons differentially integrate retinal activity in vivo is still largely unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Kaneda et al., 2008; Mize, 1992)

claim: Both excitatory and inhibitory SC neurons receive comparably strong RGC inputs.
source: Our results demonstrate that both excitatory and inhibitory SC neurons receive comparably strong RGC inputs and similar wiring rules apply for RGCs innervation of both SC cell types, unlike the cell type-specific connectivity in the thalamocortical system.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing similar efficacy values between RGC-SC EXN and RGC-SC IN pairs (Figure 2F)

claim: Similar wiring rules apply for RGC innervation of both excitatory and inhibitory SC cell types.
source: Our results demonstrate that both excitatory and inhibitory SC neurons receive comparably strong RGC inputs and similar wiring rules apply for RGCs innervation of both SC cell types, unlike the cell type-specific connectivity in the thalamocortical system.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing similar functional similarity and connection patterns between RGC-SC EXN and RGC-SC IN pairs (Figure 3)

claim: Retinal activity contributed more to the spiking activity of postsynaptic excitatory compared to inhibitory SC neurons.
source: Moreover, retinal activity contributed more to the spiking activity of postsynaptic excitatory compared to inhibitory SC neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing higher contribution values for RGC-SC EXN pairs compared to RGC-SC IN pairs (Figure 5B)

claim: The visual cortex and the SC differently integrate sensory afferent inputs.
source: This study deepens our understanding of cell type-specific retinocollicular functional connectivity and emphasizes that the two major brain areas for visual processing, the visual cortex and the SC, differently integrate sensory afferent inputs.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of retinocollicular connectivity patterns with thalamocortical connectivity patterns described in the literature

claim: The mouse superior colliculus (SC) is a midbrain structure that receives direct inputs from retinal ganglion cells (RGCs).
source: The mouse superior colliculus (SC) is a midbrain structure that receives direct inputs from retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) (Dräger and Hubel, 1976; Ellis et al., 2016; Huberman et al., 2008; Kremkow and Alonso, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: The SC plays a key role in visually guided behaviors.
source: Together with the visual cortex (Glickfeld et al., 2013; Lashley, 1931; Niell and Scanziani, 2021; Petruno et al., 2013), the SC plays a key role in visually guided behaviors (Evans et al., 2018; Hoy et al., 2019; Shang et al., 2019; Shang et al., 2015; Wei et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: The visual SC layers contain one of the highest densities of inhibitory (GABAergic) neurons in the brain.
source: Intriguingly, the visual SC layers contain one of the highest densities of inhibitory (GABAergic) neurons in the brain (Kaneda et al., 2008; Mize, 1992) suggesting that inhibition plays a key role in visual processing within the SC.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Inhibition plays a key role in visual processing within the SC.
source: Intriguingly, the visual SC layers contain one of the highest densities of inhibitory (GABAergic) neurons in the brain (Kaneda et al., 2008; Mize, 1992) suggesting that inhibition plays a key role in visual processing within the SC.
evidence: Inferred from the high density of inhibitory neurons in the SC

claim: SC inhibitory neurons are involved in surround suppression.
source: Indeed, SC inhibitory neurons (INs) are known to be involved in several sensory functions including surround suppression (Kasai and Isa, 2016) and motion processing (Barchini et al., 2018; Gale and Murphy, 2016), but also in the regulation of wakefulness (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: SC inhibitory neurons are involved in motion processing.
source: Indeed, SC inhibitory neurons (INs) are known to be involved in several sensory functions including surround suppression (Kasai and Isa, 2016) and motion processing (Barchini et al., 2018; Gale and Murphy, 2016), but also in the regulation of wakefulness (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: SC inhibitory neurons are involved in the regulation of wakefulness.
source: Indeed, SC inhibitory neurons (INs) are known to be involved in several sensory functions including surround suppression (Kasai and Isa, 2016) and motion processing (Barchini et al., 2018; Gale and Murphy, 2016), but also in the regulation of wakefulness (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: In sensory cortices, thalamic afferents differentially activate EXNs and local INs.
source: For example, in sensory cortices, thalamic afferents differentially activate EXNs and local INs (Cruikshank et al., 2007; Ji et al., 2016) with a stronger drive onto INs compared to EXNs (Bruno and Simons, 2002; Cruikshank et al., 2007; Gabernet et al., 2005; Gibson et al., 1999; Inoue and Imoto, 2006; Swadlow, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: In sensory cortices, thalamic afferents show a stronger drive onto INs compared to EXNs.
source: For example, in sensory cortices, thalamic afferents differentially activate EXNs and local INs (Cruikshank et al., 2007; Ji et al., 2016) with a stronger drive onto INs compared to EXNs (Bruno and Simons, 2002; Cruikshank et al., 2007; Gabernet et al., 2005; Gibson et al., 1999; Inoue and Imoto, 2006; Swadlow, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: The stronger drive on INs establishes an effective feedforward inhibition in sensory cortices.
source: This stronger drive on INs establishes an effective feedforward inhibition (Agmon and Connors, 1992; Bereshpolova et al., 2020; Gabernet et al., 2005; Kremkow et al., 2010a; Kremkow et al., 2010b; Sun et al., 2006) that balances the excitation from thalamic afferents (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011) and contributes to sharpening stimulus feature selectivity (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Feedforward inhibition balances the excitation from thalamic afferents in sensory cortices.
source: This stronger drive on INs establishes an effective feedforward inhibition (Agmon and Connors, 1992; Bereshpolova et al., 2020; Gabernet et al., 2005; Kremkow et al., 2010a; Kremkow et al., 2010b; Sun et al., 2006) that balances the excitation from thalamic afferents (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011) and contributes to sharpening stimulus feature selectivity (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Feedforward inhibition contributes to sharpening stimulus feature selectivity in sensory cortices.
source: This stronger drive on INs establishes an effective feedforward inhibition (Agmon and Connors, 1992; Bereshpolova et al., 2020; Gabernet et al., 2005; Kremkow et al., 2010a; Kremkow et al., 2010b; Sun et al., 2006) that balances the excitation from thalamic afferents (Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011) and contributes to sharpening stimulus feature selectivity (Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Cortical INs typically show higher firing rates compared to cortical EXNs.
source: Moreover, this wiring motif can partly be linked to the response properties of cortical INs as they typically show higher firing rates, broader tuning, low selectivity, and high sensitivity (Alonso and Swadlow, 2005; Bruno and Simons, 2002; Gibson et al., 1999; Kremkow et al., 2016; Porter et al., 2001; Swadlow et al., 2002) to facilitate feedforward inhibition in response to thalamic input.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Cortical INs typically show broader tuning compared to cortical EXNs.
source: Moreover, this wiring motif can partly be linked to the response properties of cortical INs as they typically show higher firing rates, broader tuning, low selectivity, and high sensitivity (Alonso and Swadlow, 2005; Bruno and Simons, 2002; Gibson et al., 1999; Kremkow et al., 2016; Porter et al., 2001; Swadlow et al., 2002) to facilitate feedforward inhibition in response to thalamic input.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Cortical INs typically show low selectivity compared to cortical EXNs.
source: Moreover, this wiring motif can partly be linked to the response properties of cortical INs as they typically show higher firing rates, broader tuning, low selectivity, and high sensitivity (Alonso and Swadlow, 2005; Bruno and Simons, 2002; Gibson et al., 1999; Kremkow et al., 2016; Porter et al., 2001; Swadlow et al., 2002) to facilitate feedforward inhibition in response to thalamic input.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Cortical INs typically show high sensitivity compared to cortical EXNs.
source: Moreover, this wiring motif can partly be linked to the response properties of cortical INs as they typically show higher firing rates, broader tuning, low selectivity, and high sensitivity (Alonso and Swadlow, 2005; Bruno and Simons, 2002; Gibson et al., 1999; Kremkow et al., 2016; Porter et al., 2001; Swadlow et al., 2002) to facilitate feedforward inhibition in response to thalamic input.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: SC neurons can receive strong input from RGC axons in vivo.
source: We recently demonstrated that SC neurons can receive strong input from RGC axons in vivo (Sibille et al., 2022a).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors

claim: Around one third of retinocollicular synapses connect onto INs that form intrinsic connections within the SC.
source: Moreover, around one third of retinocollicular synapses connect onto INs that form intrinsic connections within the SC (Whyland et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: RGC axonal waveforms are triphasic with a larger spatial spread.
source: RGC axonal waveforms are triphasic with a larger spatial spread (Figure 1D, left) while somatic SC neurons show a characteristic biphasic waveform profile (Figure 1D, middle and right).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Somatic SC neurons show a characteristic biphasic waveform profile.
source: RGC axonal waveforms are triphasic with a larger spatial spread (Figure 1D, left) while somatic SC neurons show a characteristic biphasic waveform profile (Figure 1D, middle and right).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Around one third (31.2%) of recorded SC neurons were GABAergic.
source: In total, we recorded 326 RGC axons and 680 SC neurons. Among the recorded SC neurons one third (31.2%) were GABAergic (Figure 1G, n=468 EXNs, n=212 INs).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G

claim: RGCs show the highest firing rate compared to SC EXNs and SC INs.
source: We found that RGCs show the highest firing rate (firing rate RGC: median = 7.55 spikes/s, Q1=2.39 spikes/s, Q3=17.93 spikes/s, n=326 RGCs; Figure 1G, bottom).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G

claim: The mean firing rate in SC INs was 1.8 times higher compared to that of SC EXNs.
source: On average, the mean firing rate in SC INs (firing rate IN: median = 3.63 spikes/s, Q1=1.6 spikes/s, Q3=8.02 spikes/s, n=212 INs) was 1.8 times higher compared to that of SC EXNs (firing rate EXN: median = 1.38 spikes/s, Q1=0.49 spikes/s, Q3=4.19 spikes/s, n=468 EXNs; SC EXN vs SC IN p=3.1567 × 10–15, SC EXN vs RGC p=4.8362 × 10–40, SC IN vs RGC p=2.7388 × 10–8, two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: Waveform classification analyses used in the cortex are not suitable for distinguishing neurons in the midbrain.
source: Similar findings have been shown in the inferior colliculus (Ono et al., 2017), a neighboring midbrain structure, suggesting that waveform classification analyses used in the cortex are not suitable for distinguishing neurons in the midbrain.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with findings in the inferior colliculus and the authors' own data

claim: 305 monosynaptically connected RGC-SC pairs were identified.
source: In total, we identified 305 connected RGC-SC pairs, of which 29.8% were retinal axons that connected onto GABAergic SC neurons (n=214 connected RGC-SC EXN pairs, n=91 connected RGC-SC IN pairs, Figure 2B, D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: 29.8% of connected RGC-SC pairs were retinal axons that connected onto GABAergic SC neurons.
source: In total, we identified 305 connected RGC-SC pairs, of which 29.8% were retinal axons that connected onto GABAergic SC neurons (n=214 connected RGC-SC EXN pairs, n=91 connected RGC-SC IN pairs, Figure 2B, D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: There is a significant difference in peak channel distance between RGC-SC EXN and RGC-SC IN pairs with longer distances between RGC axons and inhibitory SC neurons.
source: We found a significant difference in peak channel distance between RGC-SC EXN and RGC- SC IN pairs with longer distances between RGC axons and inhibitory SC neurons (p=0.03287, two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test), however, the effect size was small (Cohen's d=0.0915).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: Both SC cell types received similarly strong input from the retina.
source: Across the population, both SC cell types received similarly strong input from the retina (efficacy RGC-SC IN: median = 4.54 %, Q1=2.2 %, Q3=7.96 %, maximum = 62.05 %, n=91 connected pairs; efficacy RGC-SC EXN: median = 3.5 %, Q1=1.96 %, Q3=5.89 %, maximum = 41.12 %, n=214 connected pairs; Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: There is a positive correlation between the efficacy and the mean firing rate on the population level.
source: Surprisingly, our results demonstrate a positive correlation between the efficacy and the mean firing rate on the population level (Figure 2G, RGC-SC EXN r=0.42685; p<0.0005; RGC-SC IN: r=0.43543, p=0.00002, two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2G

claim: There is no significant difference in functional similarity between RGC-SC EXN and RGC-SC IN pairs.
source: In our data, the RGC-SC pairs span a wide range of functional similarity, however, we found no significant difference between RGC-SC EXN and RGC-SC IN pairs (similarity for RGC-SC EXN = 0.44 ± 0.15 and RGC-SC IN = 0.37 ± 0.19, n=85 RGC-SC EXN pairs, n=29 RGC-SC IN pairs, p=0.245, two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3B

claim: The synaptic efficacy was positively correlated with the functional similarity of the connected pairs.
source: The synaptic efficacy was positively correlated with the functional similarity of the connected pairs, with a stronger correlation for RGC-SC IN pairs (RGC-SC EXN r=0.37, p=0.0005; RGC-SC IN r=0.44, p=0.02, Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Functionally similar pairs are more strongly connected.
source: Overall, we observed that functionally similar pairs are more strongly connected.
evidence: Inferred from the positive correlation between efficacy and functional similarity

claim: Some SC neurons receive convergent input from a functionally more diverse pool of RGC afferents.
source: However, we also observed cases of relatively strong connected RGC-SC pairs (~10%) with low similarity (Figure 3C), suggesting that some SC neurons receive convergent input from a functionally more diverse pool of RGC afferents (Sibille et al., 2022a).
evidence: Inferred from experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Overall second retinal spikes were more efficient in driving SC activity for both RGC-SC EXN and RGC-SC IN connected pairs.
source: We found that overall second retinal spikes were more efficient in driving SC activity, and thus facilitating. This was true for both RGC-SC EXN (efficacy first RGC: median = 1.8 %, Q1=0.77 %, Q3=4.47%; efficacy second RGC: median = 2.66 %, Q1=1.16 %, Q3=6.07 %, p first vs second=3.13 × 10–25, n=214 pairs) and RGC-SC IN connected pairs (efficacy first RGC: median = 3.66 %, Q1=1.6, Q3=8.61; efficacy second RGC: median = 4.33, Q1=2.03, Q3=8.25, p first vs second=1.68 × 10–6, n=91 pairs, Wilcoxon signed-rank test) (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B and C

claim: Paired-spike enhancement has been reported in retinogeniculate and geniculocortical connections.
source: This effect is known as paired-spike enhancement and has been reported earlier in retinogeniculate (Mastronarde, 1987; Usrey et al., 1998) and geniculocortical (Usrey et al., 2000) connections.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: The majority of retinocollicular connected pairs showed paired-spike enhancement.
source: The majority of retinocollicular connected pairs showed paired-spike enhancement where second retinal spikes were more effective in driving SC response (86.45% [185/214] RGC-SC EXN pairs, 80.22% [73/91] RGC-SC IN pairs).
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: For RGC-SC EXN pairs, the second retinal spike was 1.7 times as effective in driving responses in the postsynaptic SC neuron.
source: The effect was more pronounced in RGC-SC EXN pairs where the second retinal spike was 1.7 times as effective in driving responses in the postsynaptic SC neuron, while for RGC-SC IN pairs, the second retinal spike was only 1.3 times more efficacious in driving SC spiking.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: For RGC-SC IN pairs, the second retinal spike was 1.3 times more efficacious in driving SC spiking.
source: The effect was more pronounced in RGC-SC EXN pairs where the second retinal spike was 1.7 times as effective in driving responses in the postsynaptic SC neuron, while for RGC-SC IN pairs, the second retinal spike was only 1.3 times more efficacious in driving SC spiking.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Paired-spike enhancement is stronger in RGCs connecting onto EXNs compared to INs.
source: To quantify this observation, we calculated the paired-spike ratio (PSR = efficacy second/efficacy first) which confirmed a higher facilitation effect for RGCs connecting onto EXNs (PSR RGC-SC EXN = 1.711 ± 1.14; RGC-SC IN: 1.281±0.414, p=2.58 × 10–7, Wilcoxon rank-sum, n=305 pairs, Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: In the thalamocortical system, weaker synaptic connections can be more strongly modulated compared to stronger synaptic connections.
source: Previous work in the thalamocortical system has shown that weaker synaptic connections can be more strongly modulated compared to stronger synaptic connections (Ferrarese et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: There is a negative correlation between the logarithm of the first RGC efficacy and the logarithm of PSR for both RGC-SC EXN and RGC-SC IN pairs.
source: We observed a negative correlation between the logarithm of the first RGC efficacy and the logarithm of PSR for both RGC-SC EXN (r=0.3314, p=7.0148 × 10–7, n=214 pairs) and RGC-SC IN pairs (r=0.4767, p=1.7714 × 10–6, n=91 pairs).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: The contribution of individual retinal spikes on SC activity was higher for excitatory compared to inhibitory SC neurons.
source: Interestingly, we found that the contribution of individual retinal spikes on SC activity was higher for excitatory compared to inhibitory SC neurons (Figure 5B) (contribution RGC-SC EXN: median = 18.27% Q1=10.79%, Q3=29.69%, n=214; contribution RGC-SC IN: median = 12.2%, Q1=6.61%, Q3=23.02%, n=91 connected pairs, p=0.0003, two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: SC EXNs might be more specifically linked to the retinal input compared to SC INs.
source: This opens up the possibility that SC EXNs might be more specifically linked to the retinal input compared to SC INs.
evidence: Inferred from the higher contribution values for RGC-SC EXN pairs

claim: Stronger coupled pairs show higher functional similarity.
source: To assess the relationship between the coupling strength and the functional similarity, we correlated both measures and found a positive correlation, suggesting that stronger coupled pairs show higher similarity (RGC-SC EXN r=0.541, p=8.9 × 10–8, n=85 pairs; RGC-SC IN r=0.461, p=0.012, n=29 pairs, Pearson correlation coefficient test, Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: There is a negative correlation between contribution and mean firing rate for both RGC-SC EXN and RGC-SC IN pairs.
source: And indeed, when we correlated the contribution to the mean firing rate, we found a negative correlation for both RGC-SC EXN and RGC-SC IN pairs (RGC-SC EXN r=–0.15079, p=0.02742; RGC-SC IN r=–0.48386, p<0.00001, Pearson correlation coefficient test n=214 RGC-EXN; n=91 RGC-IN connected pairs) (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5D

claim: Retinal input contributes a substantial part to the spiking activity of excitatory SC neurons.
source: Taken together, the cell type-specific difference in retinal coupling strength suggests that retinal input contributes a substantial part to the spiking activity of excitatory SC neurons, while inhibitory SC neurons seem to also integrate inputs from other sources.
evidence: Inferred from the higher contribution values for RGC-SC EXN pairs

claim: Inhibitory SC neurons seem to also integrate inputs from other sources.
source: Taken together, the cell type-specific difference in retinal coupling strength suggests that retinal input contributes a substantial part to the spiking activity of excitatory SC neurons, while inhibitory SC neurons seem to also integrate inputs from other sources.
evidence: Inferred from the lower contribution values for RGC-SC IN pairs

claim: Excitatory SC neurons are more tightly linked to the retinal input compared to inhibitory SC neurons.
source: This finding denotes that excitatory SC neurons are more tightly linked to the retinal input compared to inhibitory SC neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the higher contribution values for RGC-SC EXN pairs

claim: The retinal drive is similarly strong for RGCs connecting onto GABAergic and non-GABAergic SC neurons.
source: Our findings allow the following conclusions: (1) The retinal drive is similarly strong for RGCs connecting onto GABAergic and non-GABAergic SC neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing similar efficacy values

claim: The connection strength between the RGCs and both SC cell classes is positively correlated with their functional similarity.
source: (2) The connection strength between the RGCs and both SC cell classes is positively correlated with their functional similarity, while still allowing for the presence of strong connections with low functional similarity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing positive correlation

claim: Paired-spike enhancement in RGC-SC connections was a signature for both excitatory and inhibitory SC neurons.
source: (3) Paired-spike enhancement in RGC-SC connections was a signature for both excitatory and inhibitory SC neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing facilitation in both cell types

claim: The contribution of a retinal spike to overall SC firing is higher in excitatory SC neurons compared to inhibitory SC neurons.
source: (4) Finally, the contribution of a retinal spike to overall SC firing is higher in excitatory SC neurons compared to inhibitory SC neurons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing higher contribution values for EXNs

claim: Cortical INs are more strongly activated by thalamic axons compared to EXNs.
source: While cortical INs are more strongly activated by thalamic axons compared to EXNs (Bruno and Simons, 2002; Cruikshank et al., 2007; Ji et al., 2016), our results now show that in the SC, the afferent retinal drive is comparably strong on EXNs and INs.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: In the SC, the afferent retinal drive is comparably strong on EXNs and INs.
source: While cortical INs are more strongly activated by thalamic axons compared to EXNs (Bruno and Simons, 2002; Cruikshank et al., 2007; Ji et al., 2016), our results now show that in the SC, the afferent retinal drive is comparably strong on EXNs and INs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from this study

claim: The two major visual brain structures in the vertebrate brain, the visual cortex and the SC, integrate afferent sensory information differentially.
source: This finding is intriguing and suggests that the two major visual brain structures in the vertebrate brain, the visual cortex and the SC, integrate afferent sensory information differentially.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of retinocollicular and thalamocortical connectivity patterns

claim: SC neurons receive input from a small number (4–6) of RGCs.
source: SC neurons receive input from a small number (4–6) of RGCs (Chandrasekaran et al., 2007; Furman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Cortical neurons receive numerous (approximately one order of magnitude more) thalamic inputs that are usually weak.
source: In contrast, cortical neurons receive numerous (approximately one order of magnitude more) thalamic inputs that are usually weak (Bruno and Sakmann, 2006; Jin et al., 2011; Lien and Scanziani, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Individual RGC inputs may be sufficiently strong to drive the SC neuron.
source: Overall, we observed strong retinal drive onto both SC populations indicated by high efficacy values (Figure 2), and thus individual inputs may be sufficiently strong to drive the SC neuron.
evidence: Inferred from the high efficacy values observed in the data

claim: Thalamic drive is boosted by synchronously active thalamic inputs in the thalamocortical system.
source: This is in contrast to thalamocortical inputs, where individually efficacy values are low, but the thalamic drive is boosted by synchronously active thalamic inputs (Alonso et al., 1996; Bruno and Sakmann, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Cortical INs display higher sensitivity compared to cortical EXNs.
source: Cortical INs display higher sensitivity, receive more convergent thalamic input, have higher firing rates, and sample more randomly while EXNs receive highly functional specific thalamic input (Clay Reid and Alonso, 1995; Kyriazi et al., 1994; Simons and Carvell, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Cortical INs receive more convergent thalamic input compared to cortical EXNs.
source: Cortical INs display higher sensitivity, receive more convergent thalamic input, have higher firing rates, and sample more randomly while EXNs receive highly functional specific thalamic input (Clay Reid and Alonso, 1995; Kyriazi et al., 1994; Simons and Carvell, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Cortical INs have higher firing rates compared to cortical EXNs.
source: Cortical INs display higher sensitivity, receive more convergent thalamic input, have higher firing rates, and sample more randomly while EXNs receive highly functional specific thalamic input (Clay Reid and Alonso, 1995; Kyriazi et al., 1994; Simons and Carvell, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Cortical INs sample more randomly compared to cortical EXNs.
source: Cortical INs display higher sensitivity, receive more convergent thalamic input, have higher firing rates, and sample more randomly while EXNs receive highly functional specific thalamic input (Clay Reid and Alonso, 1995; Kyriazi et al., 1994; Simons and Carvell, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Cortical EXNs receive highly functional specific thalamic input.
source: Cortical INs display higher sensitivity, receive more convergent thalamic input, have higher firing rates, and sample more randomly while EXNs receive highly functional specific thalamic input (Clay Reid and Alonso, 1995; Kyriazi et al., 1994; Simons and Carvell, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Visual response properties between EXNs and INs in the SC may not differ to such a great extent.
source: In general, visual response properties between EXNs and INs in the SC may not differ to such a great extent (Inayat et al., 2015; Kasai and Isa, 2016; Shi et al., 2017, but see Barchini et al., 2018; Li and Meister, 2022), and experiments in the inferior colliculus show that GABAergic and glutamatergic cells share similar response properties (Ono et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: In the inferior colliculus, GABAergic and glutamatergic cells share similar response properties.
source: In general, visual response properties between EXNs and INs in the SC may not differ to such a great extent (Inayat et al., 2015; Kasai and Isa, 2016; Shi et al., 2017, but see Barchini et al., 2018; Li and Meister, 2022), and experiments in the inferior colliculus show that GABAergic and glutamatergic cells share similar response properties (Ono et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: In the SC and other parts of the midbrain, the cell type-specific difference in terms of selectivity might not be as strongly separated as in the cortex.
source: These observations imply that in the SC and other parts of the midbrain, the cell type-specific difference in terms of selectivity might not be as strongly separated as in the cortex.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of SC and cortical response properties

claim: SC neurons may show high projection specificity by integrating inputs from a functional homogeneous population of RGCs.
source: This observation suggests that SC neurons may either show high projection specificity by integrating inputs from a functional homogeneous population of RGCs (Li and Meister, 2022; Shi et al., 2017; Sibille et al., 2022a) or receive diverse inputs from multiple functional RGC types (Li and Meister, 2022; Sibille et al., 2022a).
evidence: Inferred from the data showing strong connections with high functional similarity

claim: SC neurons may receive diverse inputs from multiple functional RGC types.
source: This observation suggests that SC neurons may either show high projection specificity by integrating inputs from a functional homogeneous population of RGCs (Li and Meister, 2022; Shi et al., 2017; Sibille et al., 2022a) or receive diverse inputs from multiple functional RGC types (Li and Meister, 2022; Sibille et al., 2022a).
evidence: Inferred from the data showing strong connections with low functional similarity

claim: A high degree of projection specificity is maintained even disynaptically toward brain regions downstream of the SC.
source: Moreover, a high degree of projection specificity was recently shown to be maintained even disynaptically toward brain regions downstream of the SC (Reinhard et al., 2019), suggesting that at least one important role of the RGC-SC projection is to preserve the representation of the functionally diverse retinal channels (Baden et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: One important role of the RGC-SC projection is to preserve the representation of the functionally diverse retinal channels.
source: Moreover, a high degree of projection specificity was recently shown to be maintained even disynaptically toward brain regions downstream of the SC (Reinhard et al., 2019), suggesting that at least one important role of the RGC-SC projection is to preserve the representation of the functionally diverse retinal channels (Baden et al., 2016).
evidence: Inferred from the maintenance of projection specificity downstream of the SC

claim: Retinogeniculate connections show paired-spike enhancement.
source: While retinogeniculate connections show paired-spike enhancement (Usrey et al., 1998), thalamocortical and corticotectal synapses express mostly depressing dynamics (Bereshpolova et al., 2006; Swadlow et al., 2002; Swadlow and Gusev, 2001, but see Usrey et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Thalamocortical and corticotectal synapses express mostly depressing dynamics.
source: While retinogeniculate connections show paired-spike enhancement (Usrey et al., 1998), thalamocortical and corticotectal synapses express mostly depressing dynamics (Bereshpolova et al., 2006; Swadlow et al., 2002; Swadlow and Gusev, 2001, but see Usrey et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Retinocollicular connections facilitate.
source: Our data now reveals that retinocollicular connections facilitate, suggesting that the temporal integration of RGC inputs by SC neurons may be similar to the visual thalamus (dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus [dLGN]).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing paired-spike enhancement

claim: The temporal integration of RGC inputs by SC neurons may be similar to the visual thalamus (dLGN).
source: Our data now reveals that retinocollicular connections facilitate, suggesting that the temporal integration of RGC inputs by SC neurons may be similar to the visual thalamus (dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus [dLGN]).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of paired-spike enhancement in retinocollicular connections

claim: In the mouse, the dLGN mainly consists of relay neurons, and only approximately 6% of INs.
source: The dLGN serves as another main target of RGC axons, however, in the mouse, the dLGN mainly consists of relay neurons, and only approximately 6% of INs (Butler, 2008; Evangelio et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: RGC axons innervating the dLGN form triadic arrangements with EXNs and INs.
source: RGC axons innervating the dLGN form triadic arrangements with EXNs and INs (Sherman, 2004; Wilson et al., 1984) and this arrangement can also be found in the SC (Whyland et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Triadic arrangements can also be found in the SC.
source: RGC axons innervating the dLGN form triadic arrangements with EXNs and INs (Sherman, 2004; Wilson et al., 1984) and this arrangement can also be found in the SC (Whyland et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: GAD67 is a suitable marker to target the INs involved in the triadic motif in the SC.
source: It has been shown that GAD67 is a suitable marker to target the INs involved in the triadic motif in the SC (Whyland et al., 2020) and therefore, it would be interesting to study retinal connectivity in the context of these triads in the SC using GAD67 mice.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Retinocollicular synapses are modulated by the animals' level of arousal.
source: For future studies it would be interesting to examine connectivity dynamics and innervation strength in awake conditions as it has been shown that retinocollicular synapses are modulated by the animals' level of arousal (Schröder et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: More than 30 different types of RGCs have been characterized.
source: Likewise, more than 30 different types of RGCs have been characterized (Baden et al., 2016; Sanes and Masland, 2015) and understanding how specific RGC types relay information onto the different SC neuron types would be important to address in more detail in future studies.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Previous studies have shown a relationship between the response properties of SC neurons and their location along the dorsal/ventral axis.
source: Moreover, previous studies have shown a relationship between the response properties of SC neurons and their location along the dorsal/ventral axis (Liu et al., 2023) and differences in the density and size of retinocollicular terminals along this axis (Carter et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: There are differences in the density and size of retinocollicular terminals along the dorsal/ventral axis.
source: Moreover, previous studies have shown a relationship between the response properties of SC neurons and their location along the dorsal/ventral axis (Liu et al., 2023) and differences in the density and size of retinocollicular terminals along this axis (Carter et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: In the upper SC layers, a substantial part of neurons (30%) are GABAergic.
source: These observations are in line with previous findings showing that in the upper SC layers, a substantial part of neurons (30%) are GABAergic (Mize, 1992; Whyland et al., 2020) and that around one third of the postsynaptic targets of retinocollicular terminals are GABAergic (Boka et al., 2006; Whyland et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Around one third of the postsynaptic targets of retinocollicular terminals are GABAergic.
source: These observations are in line with previous findings showing that in the upper SC layers, a substantial part of neurons (30%) are GABAergic (Mize, 1992; Whyland et al., 2020) and that around one third of the postsynaptic targets of retinocollicular terminals are GABAergic (Boka et al., 2006; Whyland et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Four distinct classes of retinorecipient SC neurons have been identified: stellate, horizontal, WF, and NF neurons.
source: Morphologically and functionally, four distinct classes of retinorecipient SC neurons have been identified: stellate, horizontal, WF, and NF neurons (Gale and Murphy, 2016; Gale and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: NF neurons show strong direction selectivity.
source: NF neurons show strong direction selectivity (DS) suggesting that these cells might be strongly driven by the retina, likely from DS-RGCs (Gale and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: NF neurons might be strongly driven by the retina, likely from DS-RGCs.
source: NF neurons show strong direction selectivity (DS) suggesting that these cells might be strongly driven by the retina, likely from DS-RGCs (Gale and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the strong direction selectivity of NF neurons

claim: WF cells have extensive dendritic arbors and large RF sizes.
source: In contrast, WF cells have extensive dendritic arbors and large RF sizes.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about WF cells

claim: WF cells likely integrate inputs from multiple RGC axons.
source: These cells likely integrate inputs from multiple RGC axons (Gale and Murphy, 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the extensive dendritic arbors and large RF sizes of WF cells

claim: Three categories of potential GABAergic interneurons have been classified in the SC by the use of Cre-lines.
source: Three categories of potential GABAergic interneurons have been classified in the SC by the use of Cre-lines (Whyland et al., 2020) that can be further subdivided into intrinsic interneurons and potential projection neurons.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Trans-Seq is a novel approach to classify subsets of SC cell types that are innervated by genetically defined RGC types.
source: A recent study by Tsai et al., 2022, has mapped retinocollicular connectivity by targeting specific RGC-SC circuits using a novel approach (Trans-Seq) to classify subsets of SC cell types that are innervated by genetically defined RGC types (Tsai et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Five inhibitory clusters of retinorecipient SC cells have been identified using Trans-Seq.
source: They identified five inhibitory clusters of retinorecipient SC cells that allow to specifically map retinocollicular connectivity.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Tsai et al., 2022)

claim: 12 distinct inhibitory subtypes across the entire SC circuit have been recently identified using single-nucleus RNA sequencing.
source: In addition, 12 distinct inhibitory subtypes across the entire SC circuit have been recently identified using single-nucleus RNA sequencing (Ayupe et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: EXNs and INs in the two main brain areas for visual processing, the visual cortex and the SC, integrate sensory afferent inputs in different ways.
source: Taken together, our study targeted a heterogeneous population of GABAergic neurons in VGAT-ChR2 mice and our results reveal that EXNs and INs in the two main brain areas for visual processing, the visual cortex and the SC, integrate sensory afferent inputs in different ways.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from this study comparing retinocollicular and thalamocortical connectivity
